intro:
These exercises take the chapter's central claim seriously: Solana, Sei (CosmWasm), and the EVM are three answers to the same four questions, and the Rust you write to satisfy each is more alike than the platforms suggest. You start by recalling the four-question framework and the thin-shell-around-a-pure-core shape, then read the Solana counter listing closely enough to explain why the program holds no state of its own. From there you extend the instruction set, turn the comparison table into runnable code, and harden the decode boundary against a hostile caller.

The through-line is the boundary discipline Chapter 19 established for any wire format: untrusted bytes enter, get decoded into owned domain types, a deterministic handler runs, and owned results are re-encoded into bytes the runtime persists. Every chain-specific concern lives in the shell; the handler is ordinary Rust you could lift unchanged to another platform. The lab makes that discipline concrete by forcing the increment path to reject overflow before any value reaches state.

exerciseSolutions.title: Name the four questions every chain answers
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The chapter frames every on-chain platform as an answer to four questions. First, where does contract state live? Second, what does the code actually run as, meaning the execution target? Third, how is data serialized across the host boundary? Fourth, what shape is the entry point the runtime calls? Solana answers these with external accounts, SBF bytecode, Borsh, and a single process_instruction; Sei (CosmWasm) answers with a contract-owned key-value store, wasm, JSON/serde, and an instantiate/execute/query trio; the EVM answers with contract storage, EVM bytecode, the ABI, and selector dispatch. Once you have the four answers for a platform, you have its whole personality.

The shape worth memorizing is a thin shell around a pure core. Untrusted bytes arrive at the boundary, get decoded into owned domain types, a deterministic handler runs over those owned types, and the owned results are re-encoded into bytes the runtime persists. Everything chain-specific, the deserialization, the storage access, the entry-point dispatch, lives in the shell. The handler in the middle is the part you could lift unchanged to another chain.

That split answers which part is chain-specific and which is ordinary Rust: only the shell needs porting, because it speaks the chain's serialization and storage conventions, while the handler is plain deterministic Rust over owned types that knows nothing about accounts, gas, or wasm. The shell's serialization format is also the contract's real public API, since it is the only thing a counterparty can actually send you. Following Chapter 19, a wire format is a versioned public contract: once another party encodes against your Borsh layout or your JSON schema, you cannot change it without breaking them, exactly as you could not silently change a published function signature.
criteria: States the four questions as state location, execution target, host-boundary serialization, and entry-point shape.
Identifies the handler as pure, deterministic Rust over owned domain types with all chain-specific concerns in the shell.
Describes the flow: untrusted bytes are decoded into owned types, processed, then re-encoded into bytes the runtime persists.
Connects the boundary format to Chapter 19's lesson that a wire format is a versioned public contract.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the counter through the Solana account model
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The counter value lives in account.data, the [u8; 8] buffer the Account owns. Across two calls to process_instruction, that buffer is the only thing that survives; process_instruction itself owns no persistent state. It is a free function that receives data: &mut [u8] as a parameter and computes a fresh next on each call. This is the Solana model in miniature: the program is stateless code, and the runtime hands it a mutable view of account data that lives outside the program.

read_counter and write_counter stand in for a real codec, the Borsh reader and writer a deployed program would use. The listing decodes the buffer with u64::from_le_bytes and re-encodes with u64::to_le_bytes instead of pulling in a serialization crate so the example stays crate-free while still showing the exact shape of the boundary: a fixed-width, little-endian integer read from and written back to a byte buffer, the way a by-hand Borsh implementation would do it.

Tracing SetTo(41) then Increment: the buffer starts at [0u8; 8], so read_counter returns 0. The SetTo(41) arm ignores current and sets next = 41, which write_counter encodes back; after_set is 41. The second call reads 41 from the buffer, the Increment arm computes current + 1 = 42, write_counter persists it, and after_inc is 42. A final read_counter returns 42. So after_set = 41, after_increment = 42, and the final counter is 42.

process_instruction takes data: &mut [u8] rather than the Account by value because the program does not own the account; the runtime does. A mutable borrow of the buffer lets the program mutate persisted state for the duration of the call without taking ownership of it, which is precisely Solana's external-account model. Taking the Account by value would imply the program owns and could drop the account, which is exactly the relationship Solana does not have.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Asserting the traced values: SetTo(41) then Increment leaves the account buffer holding 42.
criteria: States that state lives in account.data and the program is stateless code called with a mutable view of that buffer.
Identifies from_le_bytes / to_le_bytes as a hand-rolled, Borsh-style little-endian codec standing in for a real serializer.
Trace yields after_set = 41, after_increment = 42, and final counter = 42.
Explains that the mutable borrow lets the program mutate persisted state it does not own, matching Solana's external-account model.

exerciseSolutions.title: Add a Decrement instruction with a floor at zero
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The change is local to two places: a new variant on the Instruction enum and a new arm in the process_instruction match. The decode-apply-encode structure is untouched. read_counter still pulls the current value from the buffer, the match computes a fresh next, and write_counter persists it. Nothing about reading or writing the buffer needs to change because the only thing that varies between instructions is how next is derived from current.

The one real concern is that counter values are u64, an unsigned type. Decrementing 0 with a plain current - 1 would underflow: in debug builds it panics, and in release builds it wraps to u64::MAX. Both are wrong for a counter that should floor at zero. u64::saturating_sub is the correct tool here because it clamps at the type's minimum, returning 0 rather than panicking or wrapping. This keeps the arm a single expression with no extra error path, which fits the stateless entry point.

Demonstrating it: starting from a zeroed buffer, SetTo(1) writes 1. The first Decrement reads 1, computes 1.saturating_sub(1) = 0, and persists 0. The second Decrement reads 0, computes 0.saturating_sub(1) = 0, and persists 0. A final read returns 0, confirming the floor held. The entry point still returns Result<u64, ProgramError> and the buffer remains the only persisted state.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Decrement saturates at 0 so two decrements from 1 leave the buffer holding 0, not u64::MAX.
criteria: Instruction gains a Decrement variant and process_instruction matches it without changing the read_counter / write_counter calls.
Decrementing at 0 yields 0 via saturating_sub rather than panicking or wrapping to a huge value.
After SetTo(1) and two Decrement calls the buffer reads 0.
The entry point still returns Result<u64, ProgramError> and the buffer is the only persisted state.

exerciseSolutions.title: Turn the platform comparison table into runnable code
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The point of the smart_contract_platform_compare listing is that the comparison table is already runnable data: describe maps each Platform variant to a PlatformModel holding the four facts. A lookup that answers a single question should reuse that single source rather than restating any platform fact. serialization_of takes a Platform, calls describe to get the model, and returns the serialization field. There is no second copy of the facts, so editing a field in describe propagates everywhere automatically.

Because Platform derives Copy, you can pass it by value into serialization_of and still use the same variant afterward in the loop, with no clone and no borrow juggling. That is exactly why the enum is a Copy type: the four facts are cheap discriminants, and a comparison helper should not have to think about ownership of a value this small.

The loop iterates the three variants, [Platform::Solana, Platform::SeiCosmWasm, Platform::EvmSolidity], and prints one line per platform naming its serialization format. The output reports Borsh for Solana, JSON/serde for Sei/CosmWasm, and ABI for EVM/Solidity, which matches the serialization column of the chapter's table.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: serialization_of reads one field off describe's result; the Copy enum is passed by value with no clone.
criteria: serialization_of delegates to describe and returns the model's serialization field with no second copy of the facts.
The loop covers all three variants: Solana, SeiCosmWasm, and EvmSolidity.
Output pairs each platform with Borsh, JSON/serde, and ABI respectively.
Platform stays a Copy enum, passed by value into the helper without cloning.

exerciseSolutions.title: Harden the decode boundary against a hostile increment
exerciseSolutions.solution:
current + 1 is a boundary bug, not a theoretical edge case, because the current value is decoded from an account buffer that an untrusted counterparty can set. A counter sitting at u64::MAX is valid input: nothing in the type system or the runtime forbids it. In release builds, where Rust disables overflow panics for performance, current + 1 wraps silently to 0. So a hostile caller can drive a counter to its maximum and then issue one more Increment to reset it to 0, with no error anywhere. That is an unvalidated value reaching state, the exact failure the chapter's borrow-parse-validate-then-mutate discipline exists to prevent.

The fix is to add a ProgramError::Overflow variant and switch the arithmetic to checked_add, which returns Option<u64>: Some(n) when the sum fits, None on overflow. Mapping None to the error with ok_or turns a wrapping hazard into an ordinary Result. The key ordering point is that the error must be returned before write_counter runs. Because the ? on the checked value propagates the error out of process_instruction before the write line is reached, no invalid value ever touches the buffer. Validate fully, then mutate.

Demonstrating it: initialize a buffer to u64::MAX (via u64::MAX.to_le_bytes()), call process_instruction with Increment, and it returns Err(ProgramError::Overflow). The write never ran, so a subsequent read_counter still returns u64::MAX, unchanged. The same checked_add treatment applies to any SetTo path that sums values, since those are equally driven by untrusted input.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: checked_add plus ok_or rejects overflow before write_counter, so the buffer is never mutated on the failing path.
criteria: Names the bug as an unvalidated value reaching state: a release-mode wrapping add on attacker-controlled bytes.
process_instruction uses checked_add and returns ProgramError::Overflow on overflow rather than wrapping or panicking.
The error is returned before write_counter, so the buffer is never mutated on the failing path.
Incrementing a u64::MAX buffer yields Err and a subsequent read still shows u64::MAX.

exerciseSolutions.title: Plan the Solana-to-Sei port
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Run the four questions against both platforms. State model: Solana keeps state in external accounts the runtime passes in; Sei/CosmWasm gives each contract its own private key-value store it reads and writes through a storage handle. Execution target: Solana runs SBF bytecode, Sei runs wasm; both are deterministic sandboxes, so this is a build-target change, not a logic change. Serialization: Solana uses Borsh, Sei uses JSON/serde; the boundary format differs but its role, a versioned public contract, is identical. Entry shape: Solana exposes one process_instruction, while Sei splits the surface into instantiate (constructor), execute (state-changing messages), and query (read-only views).

The concrete code that must change is confined to the shell. The entry-point dispatch changes from a single process_instruction to instantiate/execute/query, so the Increment/Add operations move into execute message variants and any read becomes a query handler. The state model changes from borrowing an external account buffer to reading and writing the contract-owned kv store through the provided storage abstraction. The serialization changes from hand-rolled little-endian Borsh decoding to serde over JSON. These three, deserialization, storage access, and entry-point dispatch, are precisely the chain-specific layer.

What stays is the deterministic handler that computes the next counter from the current one over owned domain types. That function takes a current u64 and an owned instruction value and returns the next u64 (or an Overflow error); it never mentions accounts, kv stores, Borsh, or wasm. Because it is pure ordinary Rust with no chain dependencies, it moves across platforms untouched. The port wires a different shell around the same core.

The boundary discipline holds identically on both chains regardless of format: decode untrusted bytes into owned types, validate fully (the checked_add overflow guard from the previous exercise included), and only then mutate state. And the boundary format remains a versioned public contract on both, so the JSON schema on Sei deserves the same change-control care as the Borsh layout on Solana. The format differs; the rule that no undecoded or unvalidated value reaches state does not.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Factoring the next-counter computation into a pure apply makes the Solana-to-Sei port a shell swap.
criteria: Contrasts external accounts + Borsh + process_instruction (Solana) against contract-owned kv + JSON/serde + instantiate/execute/query (Sei).
Confines the changes to the shell: deserialization, storage access, and entry-point dispatch.
Keeps the pure handler unchanged and explains why it moves across platforms.
Reaffirms decode-validate-then-mutate and a versioned boundary format as constant requirements on both chains.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
after add = 40
after increment = 41
counter = 41
overflow rejected = true
labSolution.explanation:
The completed process_instruction follows the chapter's decode-apply-validate-encode shape over a buffer the program borrows but does not own. read_counter pulls the current little-endian u64 out of the account bytes, the match computes a candidate next with checked_add, and ok_or converts an overflow (None) into ProgramError::Overflow. Crucially, that ? short-circuits before write_counter, so an invalid value never reaches state.

Walking main: data starts zeroed, so Add(40) reads 0, computes 0.checked_add(40) = Some(40), writes it, and a is 40, printing "after add = 40". Increment then reads 40, computes 40.checked_add(1) = Some(41), writes it, and b is 41, printing "after increment = 41". A read of data confirms the persisted value is 41, printing "counter = 41".

The hostile case uses a separate buffer initialized to u64::MAX. Increment computes u64::MAX.checked_add(1) = None, which ok_or turns into Err(ProgramError::Overflow), returned before any write. So bad.is_err() is true and the maxed buffer is left untouched, printing "overflow rejected = true". This is the borrow-parse-validate-then-mutate discipline made executable: no undecoded or unvalidated value ever reaches state.

reviewAnswers.question: What are the four questions the chapter says every chain answers differently, and what are Solana's answers to each?
reviewAnswers.answer: The four questions are: where does contract state live, what does the code run as (the execution target), how is data serialized across the host boundary, and what shape is the entry point the runtime calls. Solana's answers are external accounts for state, SBF bytecode as the execution target, Borsh for serialization, and a single process_instruction entry point. Knowing those four facts gives you the whole shape of a Solana program; the other platforms differ only by substituting their own answers.

reviewAnswers.question: In the Solana model, where does contract state live, and why is the program itself described as stateless?
reviewAnswers.answer: State lives in separate accounts, which the runtime passes into the program as mutable byte buffers; in the listing that is the Account's data field. The program is stateless because it owns no persistent storage of its own: process_instruction is code the runtime invokes with a borrowed, mutable view of account data it does not own. Each call decodes the current value from the buffer, computes a result, and writes it back, so the buffer, not the program, is what survives between calls.

reviewAnswers.question: What do from_le_bytes and to_le_bytes stand in for in the counter listing, and why does the chapter hand-roll them instead of using a crate?
reviewAnswers.answer: They stand in for a real serialization codec, specifically the Borsh reader and writer a deployed Solana program would use to move a u64 across the host boundary. The chapter hand-rolls the little-endian decode and encode so the example stays crate-free while still showing the exact shape of the boundary: a fixed-width integer read from and written back to a byte buffer. The mechanics are deliberately the same as a by-hand Borsh implementation, just without the dependency.

reviewAnswers.question: What does 'never let an undecoded or unvalidated value reach state' mean in practice, and in what order should you borrow, parse, validate, and mutate?
reviewAnswers.answer: It means input bytes come from a potentially hostile counterparty, so you must fully decode and check a value before it is allowed to change persisted state. The order is: borrow the input buffer, parse the raw bytes into owned domain types, validate those types (for example reject an Increment that would overflow with checked_add), and only then mutate state by writing back. The mutation step must be unreachable on any error path, so a failed validation returns before write_counter runs and the stored state is left untouched.

reviewAnswers.question: Which three facts about a contract's runtime (no ambient I/O, metered execution, re-execution by every validator) constrain the ordinary Rust you can write, and why?
reviewAnswers.answer: A contract runs in a sandbox with no ambient I/O, every operation costs a metered resource (gas), and every validator re-executes it expecting byte-identical results. No ambient I/O means you cannot read files, the clock, the network, or a random source the way a normal program would, because those are not available or not deterministic. Metered execution means unbounded loops and wasteful allocation are costs you pay per instruction, so tight, predictable code matters. Re-execution by every validator demands strict determinism: any nondeterminism would make validators disagree on the result, so the same inputs must always produce the same outputs, a discipline close to embedded programming.
